title: Stanford CS221 | Autumn 2025 | Lecture 18: AI & Society
transcriptText:
So today, we're going to talk
about AI's role in society.
So this is going to be
a bit of a departure
from the rest of the class.
So far, we've only focused on
the technical aspects of AI.
We talked about
machine learning.
We talked about
state-based models
with search MDPs and games.
We talked about
Bayesian networks.
We talked about logic.
And so now, we're going to talk
about societal implications.
And so the first
thing you might wonder
is why should we
care about this.
So this is a class about--
it's a CS class about AI.
So why are we talking
about in this class?
And there are many
other classes that you
could take to learn much
more about AI in society.
So I'll try to argue
why this is here today.
So first is
indisputably, technology
has massive impact on society.
This has been historically true.
I mean, you can go back as far
as printing press and the steam
engine and things like that.
But more recently, internet,
mobile phones, social networks
have just changed the
fabric of society,
for either better or, in
some cases, for worse.
And AI, in particular, is the
fastest growing in history.
And part of that growth
is due to the fact
that we have internet and social
media to overlay the growth
of this technology on top of.
For example, right now,
ChatGPT has 800 million
weekly active users.
And this is going
to keep on growing.
So we're in-- if
you think about,
we're only in the very beginning
stages of this technology
revolution.
The second point is that we,
as technologists, speaking
to an audience who is probably
primarily computer science,
we have an incredible
amount of power.
First, we understand the
capabilities and limitations
of this technology
better than anyone else.
We can choose what
problems to work on,
and given those systems
that we decided to build,
we make design choices
that shape access
or how the system works.
So, for example, when
building a model,
you have to decide what
languages do we support?
Or if you release, make a model,
do we release the weights?
What kind of requests
should your service take?
And which ones
should you refuse?
So as you can tell, these
are design decisions
that no one else
is going to make.
I mean, that has to be the
job of the model builder.
And these are not
technical questions.
These are design decisions
that have implications.
So if you're not convinced
yet, you can maybe
think about-- you
might be wondering,
well, we're just here to
develop the technology.
Let someone else worry about it.
That's someone else's job to
worry about the consequences.
And just to hammer it home, this
is like a relatively extreme
example.
But there was this
man by the name
of Wernher Von Braun
who in World War II,
he helped Hitler
develop rockets.
And then he came
to US and helped
develop the space program.
And the song by Tom Lehrer
sums up his perspective.
Once the Rockets are up, who
cares where they come down?
That's my department
says Wernher Von Braun.
So this is a bit--
I mean, it's a song, but I think
it describes an attitude that we
probably don't want to take.
So let's say we do care about
technological impact on society.
What should we do next?
So you can start with
now the principles.
And the broadest
principle is we want
to ensure AI is developed to
benefit and not harm society.
It almost sounds like
a platitude by now.
And there are a number
of documents you
can turn to draw inspirations.
For example, there's
a Belmont Report,
which talks about ethical
principles for human subjects
research.
And this came
about because there
was this really
unfortunate study that
was done in 1974,
where they basically
did a-- gave a batch of
African-American men, who
were known to have syphilis,
but didn't treat it
because they wanted to study.
What happens if you
don't treat syphilis?
Apparently not great things.
So that led to the creation
of the Belmont Report
to protect human
subjects research.
And the idea is that there's
some principles here.
Respect for persons, which leads
to the idea of informed consent.
Subjects have to
consent and understand
what they're getting
themselves into.
We want to maximize the
benefits and minimize the harms
and don't affect some groups
disproportionately more
than others.
All of these things were
violated in this previous study.
You can also look at things
like the ACM Code of Ethics,
which talks about, we want to
contribute to human well-being,
avoid harm, and respect
privacy and confidentiality,
and so on, and so forth.
So these all seem
pretty unobjectionable.
But the real question is, how do
we actually operationalize them
in practice?
Because it's all
well and good to say,
we want to benefit
society and minimize harm.
But what does that
actually mean?
So I'm going to talk
through a bit of let's say,
call them frameworks
to think about
and help us orient how we should
think about this, admittedly,
a very challenging problem.
So this is a question,
how do we benefit society
by developing AI?
And the main problem
here is that we don't
get to fully control its use.
If you commit a bad act,
then that's your choice.
We can say to ourselves,
don't do bad things.
But the challenge is
that that's not our call.
And AI is an example of
a dual use technology.
One that can be used to both
benefit it or to harm people.
And dual use technologies
aren't new to AI.
They've been around
for some time.
I think they were fairly--
there's this idea of dual use
as came up probably
first in when
thinking about in the chemical
industry where ammonia was
used heavily for agriculture.
But then they could also be
used for chemical weapons.
Rockets, as we saw
earlier, they can
be used to fire
missiles at people,
or they can send
people into space
and discover science
and all that.
Nuclear is probably
a prime example.
It can be used as
weapons or for energy.
Cybersecurity-- if
you have, let's say
an agent that can
hack into a server,
this can actually be useful
for penetration testing.
So testing your own servers
before you deploy them,
or they could actually
be used for cyber attacks
on someone else's servers.
And then finally, encryption.
So they can protect
user privacy.
And we all love--
encryption is the foundation
of how you can do anything
on the internet these
days, but it can also
be used to conceal
criminal activity.
In encryption, we all
take it for granted today,
but 20, 30 years ago, there was
a big debate over the dual use
of encryption and
actually was banned
or strong encryption was
banned for a bit of time.
So an AI is a dual
use technology.
But that doesn't mean you just
throw up your hands and say,
well, it could go either way.
It could be positive
or negative.
You can't do anything about it.
There are things you can
do to steer AI so that it
tilts towards the benefits.
I said it was hard, but I
didn't say it was impossible.
So the way to think about the
role of AI in impact on society
is this diagram here.
There's two axes here--
intent and impact.
An intent could be good and bad.
An impact could be
positive or negative.
So in this upper left quadrant,
you're trying to do good things
and you have a positive impact.
These are beneficial
applications
to health care, education,
science, things like that.
Then you could be in this
lower right quadrant,
where you have bad
intent and you have
a negative impact on society--
spam, fraud, and disinformation.
This is generally
about misuse of AI.
So don't do that.
The more subtle case is in this
upper right quadrant, where
you have good intent, but
somehow something happens,
and it turns out to
have a negative impact.
This is probably the more common
case in a lot of situations.
And that's something
we'll talk about.
And now, there is also this--
technically, this other quadrant
here where you have bad
intent and you end up
having good outcomes that as
far as I know, I don't know.
I guess you have to be a
pretty bad supervillain
to live in that quadrant.
Benefits-- beneficial
applications,
I think there's many things that
we can do that helps the world.
And remember, we,
as researchers,
we choose what
problems we work on.
So we can choose problems
along these lines,
I have a more direct impact.
So for example,
just to name a few,
AI will have a big influence
in the biomedical space
to accelerate drug development.
For example, AlphaFold
and its successors
not only can predict
protein structure,
but also how these proteins
bind to various kind of drugs.
And this can be used to
accelerate drug development,
because you can do a bunch
of simulations or model calls
instead of actually doing
the wet lab experiment.
More on the clinical
side, it could
be used to help doctors, for
example, answer questions
on electronic health
records, or it
could be used to communicate
with patients directly.
Let's say, translating
medical jargon into language
that one can understand.
In education, on
the student side,
you can have
personalized learning.
On the instructor side, you
could design curriculum,
create problems,
automatic grade.
The main challenge here is to
think about pedagogy rather than
task completion.
Because if you have a tutor, you
don't want it just to give you
the answer immediately.
You wanted to make
sure you understand.
Robotics-- there's self-driving
cars, which are actually, pretty
good these days.
And it seems like people are
now looking more aggressively
at other forms of robots,
such as in a household, which
would have significant
implications for countries
with large aging populations.
Weather and climate
forecasting for early warning
and monitoring the effectiveness
of various climate policies.
So all these things are
things that AI could
have a very positive impact on.
Then a few misuse.
Obviously, there's more, but
just to give you a sense.
There's cyber attacks.
So AI it can be powerful enough.
There's a recent
Anthropic post showing
that they detected
a bunch of attackers
using Claude Code to conduct
a large-scale cyber attack.
And AI agents are getting good
enough, where these things can
actually be quite effective.
Now, remember some of
the flip side of this
is that the same agents could be
helpful for securing our system
or detecting vulnerabilities.
So AI is always dual
use in this way.
We can also generate text,
images, audio, video, now,
with stunning fidelity.
And this, obviously, can be used
for spreading disinformation,
misinformation.
This can be used
by state actors.
Or it could be used
by teenagers that
want to do harm to their peers.
These are fairly big
and serious problems.
Then if we think
about accidents,
so this is really about AI
having unintended consequences.
So neither the AI developer nor
the users wants this to happen,
but it happens anyway
through, essentially,
oversight or negligence.
So there's inequality.
So AI works better or
worse for different groups.
So if you have an
accent you might
realize that voice
assistant just
may not recognize your
speech, as well as
if someone who doesn't
have an accent.
Sycophancy has been
a big problem, where
it can affirm a false
belief that a user has,
but this is especially
troubling for users
with various mental
health issues, which can
lead to self-harm, potentially.
There's over reliance.
So just to back up a little bit.
So sycophancy right.
Why is this an accident?
So it's not the case that
language model providers
want to happen.
They're fine tuning
their models.
So that is pleasant
for the user.
But as a result,
a side effect, you
get some reinforcement
of false beliefs.
For over reliance, again,
the model developers
want these models to be helpful.
But if they're too
helpful, then people
might become over dependent
and lose the ability
to critically think
for themselves.
There's a cultural
homogenization,
where AI reinforces existing
biases and stereotypes,
and AI displacing
various job functions.
So, for example, entry
level software engineers
are maybe at the level of
what Claude Code can do,
which can cause some
stress in terms of how--
for hiring of those
entry level positions.
So in summary, there's
three categories.
Benefits-- we should
do more of this.
Misuse-- we should implement
safeguards to try to prevent.
I don't think you can
prevent misuse all together,
but you can try to prevent it.
And accidents are probably
where we can do the most.
You can do much more
preventative testing
and just be careful before
you deploy an AI system.
So the other thing I
want-- another view
of AI societal
impact is thinking
about the whole ecosystem.
And this is something
that Rishi will talk about
on the next lecture.
And the starting
point is that we often
think about an AI model.
We think about a model
as and its properties,
does it generate
the correct answer?
What kind of queries
does it handle and so on?
But that's really insufficient.
I think we need to really
take an ecosystem view on AI
to understand how
AI impacts society.
So here's a picture
you have in your head.
So here's your AI system.
It interacts the world through
either upstream or downstream.
So in the case of, let's
say, a large language model,
it interacts with upstream
in that it takes data,
which are created by people.
It takes GPUs, which comes
from resources and energy
in the environment.
And the AI system
is built, and it's
deployed downstream to users.
And the use and
misuse of that AI
causes various
impacts on people.
People live on both sides
of this picture here.
So let's look at an upstream.
So AI models, especially
large language models
are created from
data and compute.
Data, it's important to remember
that they come from people.
This idea of from a model
developer's perspective,
you can have this view that,
well, the internet data is free.
It's just out there,
and I can crawl it.
But all that data is really
the product of people's labor.
And that's something
important to remember.
And compute-- it all comes
from extracting resources
from environment, whether
that be energy or materials
to build the actual data
centers and the GPUs and so on.
There's a few considerations
that are present upstream.
So you think about privacy,
where people's information
is unintentionally revealed.
Copyright, which I'll
talk about a little
bit later, where
creators might not
be appropriately compensated.
So an incentive
system is broken.
Labor practices, where workers
might be treated poorly
because AI models are fairly
data hungry and you have to,
usually, pay people to
create data for you.
And environmental impact now
that some of these AI data
center builds are
insane in scale,
this is think about carbon
emissions, water usage,
and resource extraction.
Downstream-- AI
is used by people.
And this could have positive
and negative implications.
So inequality-- so AI helps
some more than others.
It can generate toxic content
or take harmful actions.
We already talked about
over reliance and jobs.
So now in the rest
of the lecture,
I want to deep dive a
bit into a few topics.
It is impossible to cover the
whole breadth of what it means
for AI to have an
impact on society,
so I'll try to cover
a few representative
samples to give you an idea
of some of these concerns.
So let's talk about inequality.
So in 2018, there was
a very classic study
done to show what
inequality means for AI.
So this was the
Gender Shades project.
They evaluated gender
classifiers from Microsoft,
Face++, and IBM on population.
And then they stratify
based on demographic group.
So darker male, darker female,
lighter male, lighter female,
and looked at the
accuracy rates.
And what they noticed
is that there's
one group that had much lower
accuracy than the other groups.
So if you were just
measuring average accuracy,
you would think that these
systems work pretty well,
but you wouldn't
notice the oversight
that there was actually an
intersectional group here that
was getting much worse service.
One interesting thing is
that this study came out,
and then after the study,
the systems got fixed.
So one thing that's, I
think, a big takeaway here
is that this shows the power
of third-party auditing, which
can be a powerful incentive to
incentivize to get companies
to actually fix problems.
And the first step, actually,
in solving a problem
is to identify the problem.
Sounds obvious, but
I think this really--
you have to actually do it
to really see its impact.
On the technical side, how
do you reduce inequality?
Well, one thing you could
do is collect more data
for underrepresented
demographic groups.
This generally can
be costly, which
is why I think a
lot of companies
might not have the data,
too, in the first place.
You can also do some things
on the algorithmic side,
where you can upweight
underrepresented groups
in your data set.
You can use this tool
called distributional robust
optimization, which
looks at not just
the average accuracy, but the
worst case accuracy over groups.
So what you would
do is you would
maximize the worst, the minimum
accuracy over all these groups.
And that objective
function would
allow you to make sure that all
the groups have good accuracy.
Now, just as an aside,
one thing you might wonder
is gender classification
even well-defined task
given because it's ultimately
based on the image,
you're relying on superficial
features as opposed
to reaching the kind of gender
as a self-identification.
Another type of inequality
comes more at a global level.
So I think we tend to
think a lot about models
and what's happening in the US.
But if you look at,
so here's a study
that was done, where
they took this model that
was fine tuned from Llama,
which was advertised as a reward
model, which it scores,
basically, how good AI assistant
generations given
user generations.
And they evaluated
it using this reward
model, different generations
to, where are you from?
I am from country.
And this reward
model is usually used
to then post train a language
model using reinforcement
learning, as we alluded to,
Ken talked about last time.
And we see that
this is very uneven.
So higher is blue.
It's better.
Red is worse here.
And maybe not surprisingly
like US and Canada
have really high reward.
And places like Saudi
Arabia have very low reward.
So for no particularly
good reason, obviously,
this is not a particularly
fair reward model to use.
And you can imagine if you've
fine tuned on this reward model,
you're going to get some
pretty serious biases.
Another type of inequality that
happens is a bit more subtle.
This has to do with
spurious correlation.
So here's an example problem
from a few years ago.
So the task here is given
an image of an X-ray.
Try to predict whether there
is a collapsed lung or not.
So this is some bad
medical condition.
And if you look at the
accuracies here of the system,
it's not bad.
But if you take a closer
look at this image,
this is classified
as a collapsed lung.
And the researchers
noticed that there's--
see this pipe here.
This is called a
chest drain, which
is a common treatment
for a collapsed lung.
And what happened was that
the model was basically
trying to leverage the
presence of a chest drain
to predict whether it had
a collapsed lung or not.
So this is bad because
if you look at--
this, is the accuracy.
So higher is better here.
If you look at on
average, that's the blue.
So it's 0.87.
If you look at the
people with chest strain.
So these are the people who
got treated for collapsed lung.
It looks great.
But the people
who haven't gotten
treated for chest
strains, it's much worse,
which means that the people who
don't have chest strains, which
means that they actually haven't
been treated, but nonetheless
need to be treated, we're
not able to actually
predict on those folks
very well, which is bad.
So this is known as a
spurious correlation.
These are patterns in training
data that don't generalize.
All machine learning
algorithms do
is they look for
patterns in data.
And they look for
patterns or correlations.
And a spurious
correlation is one
that you see in
the training data.
And the learning
algorithm says this
is how I'm going to predict
a collapsed lung or not,
but it actually turns out not
to be the right causal variable
to latch on to.
And therefore, if you
have another condition,
it won't work.
And this affects minority
populations often the most.
And the takeaway
from all of this
is that it is really important
to not just look at one number.
You look at accuracy and
you get it up to 90%.
And you say, wow, I
made so much progress.
It is really
important to monitor
metrics on different
populations just to make sure
that you're not
essentially harming
a particular subpopulation.
So next, I want to
talk about alignment.
And alignment is about
how do we make an AI
system do what we want to do?
So sounds fairly
straightforward,
but it turns out
not to be really.
So here, if you put on your
reinforcement learning hat,
what you would do is you define
a reward function that captures
the values or what you want.
And then you train an agent to
maximize the expected reward.
So what could go wrong here?
Any ideas?
You just write
down what you want.
That reward function
is very hard
to define, especially,
in all cases.
And what happens if
you don't get it right,
you get reward hacking.
So this is an example
from old OpenAI blog post
before they started
training language models.
And this is a game
called Coast Runners,
where the goal is to race a
boat and to finish a race.
And the reward that
you have in this game
is that you're
getting points and you
get points for hitting things.
So when you do reinforcement
learning in this environment,
the agent learns this behavior,
where the boat is just
swinging around and just hitting
this boat many, many times,
and not completing
the race at all.
So this is an instance
of reward hacking,
which is where the
reward function doesn't
capture what we want.
And this is terribly
frustrating for model developer
because they're thinking just
do what I mean, not what I say,
but I'll ask-- the algorithms
can only do what you say.
This shows up in
more realistic cases.
So for example, we have a lot
of people interested in building
coding models.
And a natural reward
function for coding agent
is that you write code
that passes unit tests.
But we know that
tests are always
complete in their
coverage, which
means that just because
you pass the test,
it doesn't mean you actually
get the answer that your code is
correct.
But even if your
code is correct,
it might have other problems.
For example, it
might not be secure,
it might not be robust
to adversarial testing.
And there's this work that
evaluates language models
both on correctness
and secureness.
And even if it were
both correct and secure,
it might have other things.
For example, it might have bad
style, it might be complex,
and so on.
And it's really, really hard to
get this reward function right.
What happens if you don't get
the reward function right?
You should be cautious.
Never over optimize
your reward function.
That's incorrect.
If it's slightly incorrect,
you can optimize it a bit,
and likely, you're going
to be moving roughly
in the right direction.
But if you over
optimize, you're going
to start gaming
the reward function
and finding all sorts of devious
ways to squeak out more reward.
And this is generally
true, I think, in life.
So a second problem is
the idea that if you
think about the reward
function representing values,
the question is, whose
values are we talking about?
And there's this
idea of pluralism,
which means that different
people have different values.
So there's actually
no one reward function
that works for everyone.
For example, the view of
is it OK for governments
to moderate public
social media content?
People are divisive on this.
It's dangerous to
pick one view of this
and just fine tune your
language model to only that view
and serve it to the
world, because then you're
projecting that
view on everyone.
And so ideally,
models would represent
the diversity of
thought, of course,
within the Overton window.
You don't want to represent
maybe like fringe kind of ideas.
At the same time, models should
be personalized but not so much.
We don't want everyone living
in their own echo chamber.
And certainly, we already saw
that sycophantic language models
are a bit dangerous.
So then there's this
trade-off between how much
do you represent that diversity
of thought versus personalized
to individual user.
So again, there's no right
answer or recipe here.
The third challenge has to
do with scalable oversight.
So language models are
getting really, really good.
They can solve incredibly
complex problems.
And already, they're
generating solutions that
are hard for experts to verify.
So we had this paper
on unanswered questions
where you take a look at all the
unanswered questions on Stack
Exchange.
And we have language models
that generate the answers,
but it's hard to actually
verify whether these answers are
correct or not.
There's a few ideas
around scalable oversight.
One is that you can break down
a problem into smaller problems,
so that humans might be able
to verify individual problems.
You can use AI itself.
Because if AI is better than
humans, at least, on some tasks,
maybe you can get
a second AI that's
better than human to
keep the first AI check.
There's some ideas around debate
and constitutional AI that
are proposing that really,
the only way to address this
is to use AI to monitor
AI, which, obviously,
has some recursive problems.
Another thought is that
if you have process level
supervision or
evaluation, which means
that language model
generates a rationale
and then you check the steps,
basically, the language model
shows the work, and then
you're checking the steps.
That is generally
going to be much more
effective than looking at, did
you get the answer right or not?
There's some other things you
might imagine, for example,
formal verification.
If you can cast things in
terms of theorem proving,
then you're good.
But most problems in the
world are subtle and complex,
and you can't really do that.
So summary of all the things
that can go wrong here.
The reward function isn't
what we want exactly
leading to reward hacking.
There's actually no one reward
function in the first place.
So you have to think
more pluralistically.
And it's really hard
to even for humans
to write down a reward
function in the first place
or to provide feedback
to an agent, let alone
write down the reward function.
So you need to have some
story for scalable oversight.
So moving on to copyright.
So copyright has to do with
the upstream dependencies
on the language one,
in particular, data.
So currently, there's a lot
of lawsuits floating around
in the Gen AI space,
mostly around copyright.
And recently, there
was a settlement.
Anthropic agreed to pay
authors $1.5 billion
to settle copyright lawsuit.
And so this is,
pretty meaningful
and that this is a big issue.
So I want to take a step
back and think about how
to think about copyright.
So this will be a bit
going through basic IP law.
But I think it's important for
understanding where language
models fit into the space.
So why does copyright exist?
So copyright is part of a
framework intellectual property
law generally.
And the goal is to incentivize
creation of intellectual goods.
And the idea is that
you protect creators.
By protecting creators,
you incentivize
